title: What Are We Measuring? Rethinking Mock Exams
author: Lead Time
summary: A school leader at an IGCSE school describes how a colleague's honest review of their Year 10 mid-course mock examination window revealed a fundamental misalignment between assessment design and assessment purpose. The core argument, grounded in cognitive science and Daisy Christodoulou's marathon analogy, is that compressing a full examination season into two weeks halfway through a two-year course does not primarily measure curriculum mastery -- it measures coping under artificial pressure. The article distinguishes between retrieval-based low-stakes testing (which strengthens learning) and high-stakes full-paper replication (which assesses performance under stress, sleep management, and emotional regulation). The recommended fix is a tighter, more deliberate model: fewer papers, capped timing, adapted format -- generating cleaner diagnostic data and healthier students.
points: The purpose of a mid-course examination window should determine its design -- if the purpose is a diagnostic checkpoint to guide reteaching and retrieval, then full-length past papers under maximum time pressure are the wrong instrument.

Running a compressed mock season at full weight midway through a two-year course is like opening training with the full race: it conflates performance under artificial compression with the knowledge security and skill development that Year 10 is actually supposed to build.

When students cram ten or more papers simultaneously, Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve ensures scores reflect short-term retention rather than secure knowledge -- creating noisy data that departments cannot act on.

Wellbeing is not a second-order concern: sustained high-stakes stress across multiple subjects degrades working memory, disrupts sleep, and erodes emotional control -- producing a dataset distorted by fatigue rather than a picture of learning.

A clear diagnosis of purpose -- 'Are we forecasting grades, identifying intervention needs, checking knowledge security, building exam literacy, or testing to strengthen memory?' -- is prerequisite to any sensible assessment design, and these are different purposes requiring different designs.
quotes: The Year 10 examination window is not primarily about generating grades. Its value is in producing information that improves learning. It should function as a diagnostic mid-course checkpoint: generating valid, reliable and actionable data that helps departments identify strengths and gaps.

You do not prepare students for high-stakes exams by placing them under high-stakes exam conditions simply because it appears to be good preparation. The conditions of the race need to be introduced gradually, once the knowledge base and the conditioning that would allow genuine performance are secure enough to be meaningfully tested.

When students are revising simultaneously for ten or more formal papers, cognitive load does not just accumulate, it compounds. And they will cram the night before each paper, producing a performance shaped by short-term retention rather than secure knowledge.
A full past paper at full length is not the only marker of seriousness, and treating it as though it were conflates performance with learning in exactly the way the research warns us against.

What our review gave us was not just a reduced exam load, though it did produce that. It gave us a clearer answer to the strategic question, and an assessment model designed intentionally around that answer.
Assessment should strengthen memory, clarify gaps and guide teaching. A tighter, more deliberate model produces better data, stronger learning and calmer students.
